His medical history included systemic sclerosis diagnosed three years prior and pulmonary fibrosis. He was on prednisolone and azathioprine. There was no history of liver disease or alcohol abuse. On physical examination, his blood pressure was 95/65 mmHg, and his pulse was 90 beats per minute. Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles were noted. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. Rectal examination confirmed melaena. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 12,700/mm3, haemoglobin level of 10.9 g/dl, platelet count of 186,000/mm3, and mean corpuscular volume of 99.4 fl. Blood urea was 12.5 mmol/l, creatinine 68 μmol/l, with normal electrolytes and glucose at 6.3 mmol/l. Liver function tests revealed serum alanine aminotransferase at 12 u/l, bilirubin at 12 μmol/l, γ-glutamyl transferase at 54 u/l, alkaline phosphatase at 35 u/l, total protein at 52 g/l, albumin at 27 g/l, and C-reactive protein at 12. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Factor V Leiden mutation was absent. Hepatitis viral serology and autoantibody screen were negative, and α-1-antitrypsin levels were normal. Ferritin was 103 μmol/l, caeruloplasmin was 0.25 μmol/l, and α-fetoprotein was 0.9 kU/L. Urgent gastroscopy identified oesophageal varices, fresh blood, and clots in the stomach. During the procedure, the oesophageal varices began to bleed. Haemostasis was not achieved with sclerotherapy, necessitating the insertion of a Sengstaken tube. The patient was admitted to the High Dependency Unit, started on intravenous glypressin and antibiotics, and received a transfusion of four units of blood. A repeat gastroscopy the following day showed two columns of grade II oesophageal varices, two oesophageal ulcers likely secondary to sclerotherapy, and mild portal gastropathy. There was no evidence of any excess inflammation and no features to suggest cirrhosis or drug-induced liver disease. Overall this was essentially normal liver tissue. Ultrasound scan of the abdomen revealed a small liver with coarse texture and no focal lesion. Hepato-portal flow was demonstrated in the portal vein. The common bile duct was of normal caliber. The spleen was enlarged (bipolar length 12.8 cm). A moderate amount of free peritoneal fluid was noted. CT scan confirmed the absence of portal vein thrombosis.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A 14-month-old female presented with significant developmental delay, cardiac anomalies, preauricular tags, dysmorphic features, polysplenia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, intestinal malrotation, and hearing loss in the right ear. The patient experienced thrombocytopenia following a liver transplant. Bone marrow examination revealed complete replacement with chronic lymphocytic leukemia and a marked reduction in erythroid precursors, consistent with pure red cell aplasia. After undergoing a bone marrow transplant, the patient remained in remission. The parents exhibited no phenotypic abnormalities.

A de novo sSMC was present in all studied cells of this case. The NOR-positive sSMC was initially characterized as a derivative of chromosome 13 or 21 by application of the corresponding commercially available centromeric probes for #13/21 (D13/21Z1) and #15 (D15Z1). As a probe specific for the short arms of all acrocentric chromosomes (midi54) gave two signals on the sSMC also the probe for the centromeric regions 14 or 22 (D14/22Z1) was applied and gave one signal on the sSMC, as well. The two centromere-near probes RP11-172D7 and RP11-81B3 in 22q11.21 gave two co-localized signals, each, while the probe RP11-1058B20 in 22q11.22 was absent on the sSMC. In summary, a dic(13 or 21;22)(13 or 21pter->13 or21q11::22q11.1~11.2->22q11.21~11.22::22q11.21~11.22->22pter) was characterized.

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette: A 59-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a mass in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. She discovered the lump during self-examination a few months prior to her visit to our outpatient clinic. The mass was mobile, with no signs of skin involvement, and axillary lymph nodes were not palpable. A recent mammogram revealed a 3.5 cm lobulated, well-defined mass, with characteristics suggestive of a fibroadenoma and no indications of malignancy. Ultrasound imaging showed a solid, hypoechoic, well-circumscribed mass measuring 3.5 cm in diameter. Blood tests indicated elevated Ca 15-3 levels. The same lesion, though less than half its current size, was initially detected on a mammogram performed in her hometown four years earlier. At that time, it was not clinically palpable and was considered a long-standing benign fibroadenoma, so it was not removed. Comprehensive staging investigations, including liver function tests, chest x-ray, CT scans of the chest and abdomen, and bone scanning, all returned negative results. The patient underwent an excisional biopsy, which revealed an invasive carcinoma. On macroscopic examination the tumour measured 3.5 cm in diameter, had solid composition and polymorphic appearance, with tan and brown, pale and hemorrhagic areas. Microscopic examination showed an invasive adenocarcinoma of the breast, characterized by average-sized cells, with well-defined borders and polygonal, rather than rounded contours. The neoplastic cells formed a matrix of solid, lobular, acinar and rarely papillary areas, with a fine vascular network in between. Foci of linear, trabecular and tubular growth patterns were visible. A few ducts with an intraductal (in situ) carcinoma of solid type were also noticed. The cytoplasm was clear and eccentrically placed and hyperchromatic nuclei with a low mitotic number (2 mitoses per 10HPF) were detected. Cells with mildly eosinophilic cytoplasma, nuclear pleomorphism and higher mitotic number were also seen. There was absence of necrosis and no lymphovascular invasion was noticed. On histochemical examination, many of the above cells were positive for PAS staining erased by diastase pre-treatment, keratins AE1/AE3, EMA and Cytokeratin 7, but negative for c-erb-b2 (score 0), Cytokeratin 20, melanosomes and vimentin. Markers of myoepithelial cells were also negative: smooth muscle actin-SMA and S-100 (only a few isolated positive cells). Staining for Chromogranin was positive in some cells and for Synaptophysin in most cells, indicating a degree of neuroendocrine activity of the tumor. The tumor was strongly positive for estrogen receptors (ER) and negative for progesterone receptors (PgR).

cases.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
cases.vignette:
A 72-year-old male patient presented with right flank pain and significant hematuria accompanied by clot retention. The patient had a history of heavy smoking but no history of trauma, recent medical procedures, or known kidney stones. He reported no bleeding disorders and was not on any medications. His blood pressure, blood count, biochemical, and coagulation parameters were all within normal limits. A rinsing catheter was used, and the hematuria resolved within a few days. Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder showed no abnormalities. A subsequent CT scan revealed a small soft tissue mass within the right renal pelvis, which did not show significant enhancement after contrast medium injection, and there was no dilation of the renal unit. No urinary tract stones or other pathologies were observed. The CT scan could not distinguish between a blood clot and a tumor. Despite the presence of a filling defect in the renal pelvis, which showed slight enhancement, the possibility of an urothelial lesion was considered. Urine cytology results were negative. A cystoscopy with the insertion of a ureteral catheter into the right pelvis was performed to selectively obtain a urine sample for cytology and conduct a retrograde study. Both cystoscopy and upper tract cytology were negative for high-grade bladder tumors. The retrograde study of the right ureter and pelvicaliceal system showed no filling defect in the right renal pelvis and calyces. Based on these findings, the CT findings were attributed to a blood clot in the right renal pelvis, and further investigation proceeded.

Selective right renal arteriography demonstrated an area of tortuous, coiled vascular channels with early filling of the renal vein within two seconds after the start of the injection.

cases.vignette: A 21-year-old male presented with an enlarged right upper limb and difficulty in function. The right arm had been larger than the left since birth, with occasional pain and swelling. These symptoms worsened when the limb was lowered. Examination revealed multiple distinct swollen areas over the entire arm and shoulder girdle, varying in size, soft, compressible, and significantly reduced in size when elevated. The right arm was shorter than the left due to overall shortening rather than localized shortening. The muscles of the arm and shoulder girdle were atrophic. The palm exhibited a bluish discoloration. No abnormalities were noted in other parts of the body. Peripheral pulses were palpable and equal in volume on both sides. The bones of the forearm and hand were underdeveloped and tender. Sensory function was intact. Muscle strength in the right upper limb was graded III to IV according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. No bruits or thrills were detected, and there was no temperature difference. The elbow could fully flex but had restricted extension, fixed at 80 degrees of flexion. The cardiovascular system was normal. Blood tests showed normal results. Radiographs showed multiple soft tissue swellings and hypotrophy of the bones of right upper limb. There were multiple well-defined radio-opaque lesions consistent with phleboliths in the affected upper limb and periscapular region. Musculoskeletal ultrasound showed multiple dilated tortuous anechoic lesions involving the upper limb and periscapular region. Echogenic lesions with shadowing suggestive of phleboliths were seen inside the anechoic lesions. The forearm muscles were thinned and replaced by these anechoic lesions. Color Doppler study showed no flow within the lesion but, while performing a Valsalva maneuver, there was sluggish flow within the lesion suggestive of dilated torturous venous channels involving the superficial venous system. The proximal part of the deep venous system appeared normal but the distal part was not visualized. The arterial system appeared normal. An MRI study showed multiple dilated veins in the superficial aspect of the right upper limb. The muscles of the limb were replaced by an abnormal signal. The triceps, biceps and deltoid were partially involved. No intra-osseous venous malformation was seen. The arteries were normal.

She had a history of heart disease and had been receiving treatment for the past four years. Clinical examination revealed a firm, mobile, non-tender lump measuring 3 × 2 cm in the outer quadrant of her left breast. The skin, nipple, and areola of the affected breast appeared normal, and there was no significant lymphadenopathy in the axillary or cervical regions. The right breast was unremarkable. Mammography showed a 2 × 2 cm ill-defined mass with irregular margins in the left upper outer quadrant, without micro-calcifications. The right breast was normal. The lumpectomy specimen displayed a firm, grey-white, fibrous, un-encapsulated nodular tumor measuring 2 × 1.2 × 0.8 cm with infiltrative borders and no calcification. The closest margin was 0.5 cm from the tumor at the base. Frozen sections showed a tumor with predominant spindle cells exhibiting mild atypia within a sclerotic stroma, infiltrating the adjacent fat. A sentinel lymph node biopsy and/or axillary node dissection were not performed during surgery. Histological sections revealed a spindle cell tumor showing an infiltrative growth pattern with prominent areas of sclerosis reminiscent of keloid formation. The cells were mainly arranged in fascicles and displayed tapering nuclei with mild anisonucleosis. Mitoses were inconspicuous. Occasionally, the cells were plump with epithelioid shapes and revealed mild atypia with an occasional small cluster formation. Interspersed were foci of benign ductal hyperplasia and papillary hyperplasia, including a micropapilloma along with focal aggregates of chronic inflammatory cells. The micropapilloma did not show any significant atypia. No discrete squamous differentiation was identified. No focus of Ductal-carcinoma-in-situ (DCIS) was seen in any of the sections. The tumor cells were simultaneously diffusely positive for epithelial markers i.e. the various cytokeratins CK, CK7, High molecular weight (HMWCK) and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), along with a mesenchymal marker i.e. vimentin. All the cytokeratins were positive in the interspersed benign ducts that acted as internal controls. The tumor cells were negative for Gross cystic disease fluid protein (GCDFP), estrogen (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR). The myoepithelial markers i.e. smooth muscle actin (SMA) and p63 showed focal, positive expression. S100 and Desmin were negative. Ki-67 (proliferation marker) showed focal positivity in less than 5% tumor cells. The tumor cells were negative for CD34 and CerbB-2/HER-2/neu. Ultrastructurally, the tumor cells embedded in a collagenous stroma showed fibroblastic and myoepithelial features along with presence of peripheral villous processes with a focal basal lamina and intercellular junctions.

cases.vignette: A 40-year-old para four obese Caucasian woman with a two-year history of lower abdominal pain was referred for further management of bilateral adnexal masses. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a complex cystic lesion of 7–8 cm in the right adnexum and bilateral ureteric obstruction. Baseline blood tests, including hematology and tumor markers (CA 125 -26 IU/ml), were normal. Serum tests indicated normal liver function and moderately impaired renal function (creatinine 10–15, urea > 200). Her medical history includes obstructive sleep apnea, asthma, glaucoma, hypothyroidism, hypertensive cardiomyopathy, and bipolar disorder; she is registered disabled. She had a copper intrauterine contraceptive device in place for the past three years. Due to her body habitus (BMI 42), abdominal and pelvic examination was challenging and non-specific, with the only notable finding being bilateral adnexal fullness. She was managed within the gynecological oncology multidisciplinary framework (MDT). CT films revealed bilateral basal pleural thickening, bilateral hydronephrosis, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy associated with retroperitoneal fibrosis, and bilateral adnexal cystic masses. A small volume of ascites was also noted. MRI was performed for further characterization of the adnexal masses. The right adnexal complex cystic lesion measured 8 × 7 × 7 cm in diameter with a thick, irregular wall (up to 2 cm) and several septations (3–4 mm). There were no enhancing papillary formations, although the wall and septa enhanced. The appearance suggested an ovarian lesion with possible involvement of the Fallopian tube. The left adnexal cyst measured 5 × 6 × 4 cm, had a smooth wall, and contained a single thin septation, consistent with a benign ovarian cyst. Both cysts contained fluid that was low on T1 and high on T2, with no evidence of fat or blood. Surrounding the cysts posteriorly, the fat appeared streaky, and there was marked thickening of the adjacent fascial planes, including the mesorectal fascia up to 1 cm. The fascial thickening extended up the pre-sacral space and along the posterior aspect of the pelvic sidewalls, causing ureteral obstruction. Enlarged lymph nodes (up to 1.8 cm in short axis) were present along both pelvic sidewalls, notable for their very high T2 signal intensity. Nodes were also observed in the inguinal and para-aortic regions. The MDT recommended clinical review and imaging-guided biopsy of lymph nodes. Histology revealed non-caseating granulomatous lymphadenitis with negative stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungi.

cases.vignette: A 75-year-old Hawaiian-Chinese female with a history of aortic stenosis, chronic renal insufficiency, and hypertension presented with pitting edema in both lower extremities. On March 21st, 2005, a cardiac catheterization revealed an ejection fraction of 15%, severe aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, and mitral regurgitation. During the procedure, venous and arterial sheaths were flushed with approximately 250 units of heparin each. Ten days later, she underwent elective aortic valve replacement and mitral valve repair surgery with intraaortic balloon pump (IABP) placement. During cardiopulmonary bypass, she received 32,000 units of heparin. Her preoperative platelet count of 108 × 10^9/L dropped to 25 × 10^9/L by the third postoperative day. She was given 12 units of random donor platelets and norepinephrine for blood pressure support. The decrease in platelets was linked to the IABP, which was subsequently removed. The patient experienced bleeding from the femoral insertion site and further hypotension, necessitating surgical repair of the femoral artery. During this surgery, she received 18 units of random donor platelets, 8 units of packed red blood cells, and 4 units of fresh frozen plasma. Her renal function worsened, requiring continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD). A heparin-flushed dialysis catheter was placed, and additional heparin was used in the CVVHD tubing circuit. Seven days postoperatively, the platelet count remained low (43 × 10^9/L) despite a total of 48 units of random donor platelets transfused. Differential diagnostic considerations included accelerated platelet removal due to CVVHD and sepsis-related disseminated intravascular coagulation. Two days later, cyanosis of the right hand was observed and attributed to a right radial arterial catheter, which was removed the next day without improvement. By then, severe ischemic changes were noted in all toes and fingers. Two days later, the platelet count reached its lowest point (8 × 10^9/L), leading to additional platelet transfusions. Heparin-platelet factor 4 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) proved strongly positive.

cases.vignette:
A 63-year-old woman reported a three-year history of a painless enlarging mass in the groin area, accompanied by increasing pain in her left leg over the past year. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) identified a lesion measuring 11 × 7 × 7 cm near the left hip, involving the quadriceps. A total body scan showed no evidence of distant metastasis.

Excisional biopsy was done, resulting in a low-grade fusocellular tumor with hemangiopericytic pattern. Grossly the tumor appeared as an encapsulated, tan-grey mass measuring 10 × 4 × 3 cm. At cut section the tumor was pseudolobulated, with small hemorrhagic foci, and yellow necrosis. No differences in color and consistence were found between lobules. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of a proliferation of fusocelular cells with haphazardly distribution and varying degrees of stromal collagenization. The cellularity greatly varied in different areas with a predominance of hypercellular areas. Medium-sized thin-walled blood vessels in a hemangiopericytic growth pattern were observed, being more evident in hypercellular areas at the periphery of the lobules. Highly cellular spindle cell areas resembled fibrosarcoma and very occasionally multinucleated cells were seen. Mitosis were spare (≤ 2 mitosis in 10 HPF) but foci of coagulative necrosis existed. At the periphery of the tumor and close to hypercellular areas we found three isolated and fairly well demarcated nodules each one measuring 12–15 mm, where cells adopted an epithelioid morphology with round, vesicular nuclei with micro nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. These cells were mainly arranged in solid sheets but nests, pseudoglandular, or cleft patterns were also present. Focally artifactual shrinkage produced pseudovascular spaces. In these areas pleomorphism was moderate. No fusocellular cells were seen. Mitosis score was more than 10 in 10 HPF, some of them abnormal, and foci of necrosis were observed. A thin band of collagen isolated these epithelioid nodules from the fusocelular rich areas except in one of the nodules which both epithelioid and spindle areas merged in indistinct transition. Cells from fusocelular and epithelioid areas showed the same immunophenotype expression: vimentin +, CD34 +, CD99 +, and bcl2 +, being completely negative for epithelial, neural and muscular markers. Ki67 immunolabeling was low in fusocellular areas (< 5%) and rather high (> 40%) in epithelioid ones. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for presence of a SYT-SSX1 or SYT-SSX2 fusion transcript proved negative.

cases.vignette: A 49-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease due to diabetes, who had been on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis for 22 months, underwent a live-unrelated kidney transplantation in April 2006. For the first six months post-transplantation, her clinical course was stable without any rejection episodes. She was on a regimen of cyclosporine (4 mg/kg/day), mycophenolate mofetil (2 g/day), and prednisolone (5 mg/day). Five months post-transplantation, she developed cellulitis in her right leg following minor trauma and was treated with intravenous cefazolin (4 g/day) and ceftriaxone (2 g/day). Although the cellulitis symptoms initially improved, three weeks later, she developed multiple painful, erythematous, firm nodules ranging from 2 to 7 cm in diameter on the anterior and posterior aspects of her right leg and lower right thigh, with some nodules becoming ulcerated. The patient had a fever of 39°C, blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg, and a regular pulse rate of 80/min. There was no edema or lymphadenopathy, and her systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL, a total white cell count of 100,000/mm3, and an ESR of 125 mm for the first hour. Serum biochemistry showed a creatinine level of 1.1 mg/dL, fasting blood sugar of 191 mg/dL, uric acid of 2.6 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase of 625 IU/L. She tested negative for cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM but positive for CMV IgG, consistent with her pretransplantation status. A chest X-ray was unremarkable. MRI of the right leg indicated severe thickening of the superficial soft tissue and skin, with no involvement of deep soft tissue or muscular structures. Histological examination of deep incisional biopsies of some of the nodules revealed lobular panniculitis with infiltrating lymphocytes, neutrophils, multinucleated giant cells, foamy macrophages, fat necrosis and granulation tissue. Hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) and periodic acid schiff (PAS) staining showed numerous broad, aseptate and irregularly branched fungal hyphae deposited within the hypoderm and vessel wall.
